# Brake Caliper Assembly with Service and Park Brake Mechanisms

## Caliper Structure

The brake caliper (100) is constructed from two principal components: a first part (104a) and a second part (104b). These parts are configured to receive a pair of braking members (102a, 102b) between them, positioning the braking members on either side of a brake disc. This arrangement allows the caliper to straddle the disc and apply clamping forces from both sides during braking operations.

## Service Brake Mechanism

The service brake mechanism is responsible for the primary, day-to-day braking function of the assembly. It employs at least two piston and cylinder assemblies arranged in an opposed configuration. This opposed-piston design enables braking forces to be applied symmetrically from both sides of the disc. When actuated, each piston and cylinder assembly drives its respective braking member toward the brake disc, generating the frictional force required to decelerate or stop the associated wheel.

## Park Brake Mechanism

Operating independently of the service brake, the park brake mechanism provides a means of holding the vehicle stationary when parked. This mechanism incorporates an actuator mechanism (112) that generates and applies a driving force to the first opposed braking member (102a), urging it toward the brake disc. In this way, the park brake can engage the disc to maintain a static braking condition.

## Force Transmission

To ensure that the park brake applies a balanced clamping force across both sides of the brake disc, a force transmitting member (116) is provided. This member transmits the driving force generated by the actuator from the first braking member (102a) to the second opposed braking member (102b). As a result, both braking members are drawn against the disc, distributing the clamping load evenly and improving the effectiveness of the park brake function.

## Support and Guidance of the Force Transmitting Member

The force transmitting member (116) is supported and guided by two sliding connections that permit controlled movement during actuation. The first sliding connection is established with the outer surface of a first cylinder (110a), while the second sliding connection engages a connecting member that spans both parts of the caliper. These sliding connections locate the force transmitting member accurately within the assembly, allowing it to translate smoothly as it transfers the driving force between the two braking members, while maintaining structural stability across both parts of the caliper.

# Brake Caliper Design with Integrated Service and Park Brake Mechanisms

## Overview

The present disclosure relates to a brake caliper design that integrates both a service brake mechanism and a park brake mechanism within a unified assembly. This design addresses the need for a compact, efficient braking system capable of delivering reliable performance in both normal operating conditions and parking applications.

## Service Brake Mechanism

The service brake mechanism employs opposed piston and cylinder assemblies to generate the clamping force necessary for controlled deceleration during normal vehicle operation. In this configuration, pistons are arranged in opposition to one another, each housed within a corresponding cylinder. When hydraulic pressure is applied, the opposed pistons advance toward a rotor or disc positioned between them, applying balanced braking forces on both sides. This opposed arrangement ensures even distribution of the clamping load and promotes consistent, symmetrical braking performance.

## Park Brake Mechanism

Complementing the service brake, the park brake mechanism provides a means of maintaining a stationary vehicle position without reliance on continuous hydraulic pressure. This mechanism utilizes an actuator that drives a first braking member into engagement. Rather than acting on only one side of the rotor, the design incorporates a force transmitting member that relays the actuation force from the first braking member to the opposing braking member. In this way, the park brake is able to apply clamping force across both sides of the rotor, mirroring the balanced action achieved by the service brake.

## Unique Support of the Force Transmitting Member

A distinguishing feature of this design lies in the manner in which the force transmitting member is supported. The force transmitting member is guided by two sliding connections. The first sliding connection engages the outer surface of a first cylinder, allowing the member to translate smoothly along this surface as parking force is applied. The second sliding connection engages a connecting member that spans the two parts of the caliper.

By supporting the force transmitting member at these two locations—one referenced to the first cylinder and the other referenced to the connecting member that bridges the caliper halves—the design achieves stable, well-guided movement of the transmitting member. This dual sliding support arrangement enables the parking brake force to be effectively distributed across the opposed braking members, ensuring that both sides of the rotor receive balanced clamping force during park brake engagement.

## Advantages

Through this configuration, the caliper design combines the reliability of opposed piston service braking with an efficiently integrated park brake mechanism. The unique support of the force transmitting member allows parking forces to be transmitted and balanced across the opposed braking members without introducing undue mechanical complexity, resulting in a robust and effective braking solution suitable for demanding applications.

## Brake Caliper with Integrated Service and Park Brake Mechanisms

A brake caliper assembly (10) is disclosed for selectively applying braking force to a brake rotor (12) positioned within a caliper body (14). The caliper body (14) defines a bore (16) housing a piston (18) that is axially displaceable to urge a pair of brake pads (20, 22) into frictional engagement with opposing faces of the brake rotor (12). 

The assembly (10) includes a service brake mechanism (24) comprising a hydraulic chamber (26) in fluid communication with a pressure port (28), wherein pressurized hydraulic fluid introduced through the pressure port (28) acts upon the piston (18) to generate a service braking force during normal operation.

A park brake mechanism (30) is integrated within the caliper body (14) and includes an actuating shaft (32) rotatably supported therein and operatively coupled to a ramp assembly (34). The ramp assembly (34) comprises a plurality of rolling elements (36) disposed between opposed ramped surfaces (38, 40), such that rotation of the actuating shaft (32) causes axial translation of the rolling elements (36) to mechanically advance the piston (18) toward the brake rotor (12), thereby applying a park braking force independently of the hydraulic pressure.

A return spring (42) biases the piston (18) toward a disengaged position, and an adjustment mechanism (44) compensates for brake pad (20, 22) wear to maintain a substantially constant clearance between the brake pads (20, 22) and the brake rotor (12). A lever (46) coupled to the actuating shaft (32) permits manual or cable-driven engagement of the park brake mechanism (30). The integrated configuration provides both dynamic service braking and static park braking within a single compact caliper body (14).

# Technical Summary: Opposed-Piston Brake Caliper with Integrated Park Brake Actuator

## Overview

This brake caliper assembly provides both service braking and parking brake functionality through a fixed-mount opposed-piston configuration. The design integrates a mechanically actuated park brake system that transmits clamping force between braking members using a sliding connection mechanism.

## Caliper Body and Service Brake Configuration

The caliper employs a **fixed (non-floating) caliper body** that straddles the brake disc (rotor). The service brake system comprises **two opposed piston-and-cylinder assemblies** positioned on either side of the rotor:

- **Inboard piston-and-cylinder assembly** — houses a hydraulic piston that advances an inboard brake pad toward the rotor face
- **Outboard piston-and-cylinder assembly** — houses a corresponding piston that advances an outboard brake pad against the opposite rotor face

During service braking, hydraulic fluid pressure is applied simultaneously to both cylinders, driving the opposed pistons inward to generate a balanced clamping force. This symmetric arrangement eliminates the need for caliper sliding motion and provides even pad wear and consistent brake torque.

## Park Brake Actuator

The park brake function is achieved through a **mechanical actuator** that operates independently of the hydraulic service brake circuit. Key characteristics include:

- The actuator **transmits force between two braking members** (e.g., between an actuating member on one side and a reaction member or piston on the opposite side).
- Force transmission is accomplished via a **sliding connection** that permits relative axial displacement between the coupled members while maintaining the load path.
- The sliding connection allows the actuator to accommodate tolerances, thermal expansion, and progressive pad wear without compromising the applied clamping force.

## Sliding Connection Mechanism

The sliding connection serves as the critical interface for park brake force transmission. It enables one braking member to translate relative to the other along a defined axis, ensuring:

1. **Load transfer** — clamping force generated by the park brake actuator is directed across the rotor to engage both brake pads.
2. **Wear compensation** — the sliding interface adjusts to maintain effective engagement as friction material diminishes over the service life.
3. **Mechanical retention** — when the park brake is applied, the connection holds the braking members in a clamped state, maintaining static holding torque without continued external input.

## Functional Advantages

- **Dual functionality** in a compact, rigid caliper package
- **Balanced braking loads** from the opposed-piston arrangement
- **Reliable park brake holding** through the mechanical actuator and sliding connection
- **Reduced maintenance** due to accommodation of wear and thermal effects

---

*Note: This is a general technical description. Specific dimensions, materials, actuation ratios, and geometric details would be defined by the particular design specification or drawing set.*

# ABSTRACT

A vehicle brake caliper (10) comprising a caliper housing (12) that supports a service brake (20) and a park brake (40) for selectively applying a braking force to a rotor (14). The service brake (20) includes a first braking member (22) actuated by a hydraulic piston (24) received within a bore (26) of the caliper housing (12) to urge a first friction pad (28) against a first face of the rotor (14). The park brake (40) includes an actuation mechanism (42), such as a motor-driven spindle (44) and nut assembly (46), operable to generate a park brake force independently of hydraulic pressure. The park brake force is transmitted from a first braking member (22) to a second braking member (32) via a force-transmitting element (50), such that engagement of the park brake (40) urges the second friction pad (34) against a second face of the rotor (14) and clamps the rotor (14) between the first and second friction pads (28, 34). A biasing member (52) may return the first braking member (22) toward a released position upon disengagement of the park brake (40). The arrangement permits a compact caliper (10) in which both service and park braking functions share common friction pads (28, 34), thereby reducing the number of components and packaging space.

A disc brake caliper comprising a first part and a second part configured to hold a pair of braking members on opposite sides of a brake disc. The caliper includes a park brake force transmitting member that applies a clamping force to actuate the braking members during a parking brake operation. The park brake force transmitting member is supported by a plurality of sliding connections that permit relative displacement between the first and second parts while maintaining alignment of the force transmitting member. The sliding connections guide movement of the park brake force transmitting member such that park brake forces are transmitted between the first and second parts to urge the braking members into engagement with the brake disc.
